questions.q: What are the SI base units of force?
questions.why: F = ma, so N = kg × m s⁻².

questions.q: A length is measured as 2.50 ± 0.05 m. What is the percentage uncertainty?
Which pair contains one scalar and one vector?
questions.why: Work is a scalar; momentum is a vector.

questions.q: When two quantities are multiplied, their percentage uncertainties are…
questions.why: For products and quotients, add the percentage uncertainties.

questions.q: Which is the SI base unit of intensity?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some used the ampere because the symbol I is used for both. Intensity is W m⁻² = kg s⁻³ in base units.

questions.q: Which of the following is equivalent to the SI unit of electric potential, the volt (V)?
questions.why: Potential difference is work done per unit charge (V = W / Q), so 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.

long.q: A student measures the length of a pendulum as 0.800 ± 0.002 m and its period as 1.80 ± 0.02 s. The acceleration of free fall is given by g = 4π²l/T². Calculate g and its absolute uncertainty.
scheme: C1: percentage uncertainties 0.25% and 2 × 1.1% = 2.2%
C1: total about 2.5%, so Δg ≈ 0.24

long.q: The drag force F on a small sphere of radius r moving at speed v through a fluid is given by F = 6πηrv, where η is a property of the fluid. Determine the SI base units of η.
scheme: B1: units of F are kg m s⁻²
M1: η = F ÷ (6πrv), so units are kg m s⁻² ÷ (m × m s⁻¹)
A1: kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹

long.q: An aircraft has a velocity of 220 m s⁻¹ due north relative to the air. A wind blows towards the east at 40 m s⁻¹. Calculate the magnitude of the resultant velocity of the aircraft and its direction relative to north.
scheme: C1: magnitude = √(220² + 40²)
A1: 224 m s⁻¹
A1: direction tan⁻¹(40 ÷ 220) = 10° east of north
long.ans: 224 m s⁻¹ at 10° east of north

long.q: Explain the difference between a systematic error and a random error in a measurement. For each, state one way in which its effect on the final result can be reduced.
scheme: B1: systematic error: readings all differ from the true value by the same amount or in the same direction (e.g. zero error)
B1: reduced by correcting for it, e.g. checking for and subtracting the zero error, or calibrating the instrument
B1: random error: readings scatter unpredictably about the true value
B1: reduced by repeating readings and averaging (or plotting a graph and drawing a best-fit line)

long.q: Make a reasonable estimate of the kinetic energy of an adult sprinter running at top speed. Show the values you use.
scheme: B1: mass of sprinter estimated in the range 50–100 kg
B1: top speed estimated in the range 8–12 m s⁻¹
A1: kinetic energy = ½mv² giving a value in the range 2 × 10³ J to 7 × 10³ J

questions.q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest at 2.0 m s⁻² for 5.0 s. How far does it go?
A ball is thrown horizontally off a cliff. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal velocity…
questions.why: No horizontal force acts, so horizontal velocity is constant; only the vertical velocity changes.

questions.q: The gradient of a displacement–time graph gives…
questions.why: Velocity = rate of change of displacement.

questions.q: An object is dropped from rest. How fast is it moving after falling 20 m? (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
A ball is kicked at 12 m s⁻¹ at 50° above the horizontal. What is the initial vertical component of its velocity?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates often used 12 m s⁻¹ as the vertical component rather than 12 sin 50°.

questions.q: A projectile is launched with velocity v at an angle θ to the horizontal. What is its acceleration at the highest point of its trajectory?
questions.why: Gravity acts downwards throughout the flight; at the top, vertical velocity is zero but acceleration is still g downwards.

long.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 15 m s⁻¹ from the top of a cliff 45 m high. Air resistance is negligible. Calculate the time taken to reach the sea and the horizontal distance travelled. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: C1: horizontal distance = 15 × t

long.q: A car is travelling at 25 m s⁻¹ when the driver sees an obstacle. The driver's reaction time is 0.70 s, after which the brakes give a uniform deceleration of 6.5 m s⁻². Calculate the total distance travelled from the moment the driver sees the obstacle until the car stops.
scheme: C1: distance during reaction time = 25 × 0.70 = 17.5 m
C1: braking distance from v² = u² + 2as: 0 = 25² − 2 × 6.5 × s
A1: braking distance = 48.1 m
A1: total = 66 m

long.q: A cyclist accelerates uniformly from rest to 8.0 m s⁻¹ in 5.0 s, travels at this constant velocity for 20 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 4.0 s. Calculate the initial acceleration and the total distance travelled.
scheme: A1: 1.6 m s⁻²
C1: distance = area under the velocity–time graph = 20 + 160 + 16

long.q: A stone is thrown vertically upwards at 12 m s⁻¹ from a point 1.5 m above the ground. Air resistance is negligible. Calculate the maximum height the stone reaches above its point of release and the time from release until it hits the ground. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: C1: v² = u² + 2as with v = 0: 0 = 12² − 2 × 9.81 × h
C1: −1.5 = 12t − ½ × 9.81 × t² (taking up as positive)

long.q: A ball is kicked from level ground with a velocity of 18 m s⁻¹ at 35° above the horizontal. Assuming air resistance is negligible, calculate the time of flight and the horizontal range. Then state and explain one effect that air resistance would have on the range. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: C1: vertical component = 18 sin 35° = 10.3 m s⁻¹ and horizontal component = 18 cos 35° = 14.7 m s⁻¹
A1: time of flight = 2 × 10.3 ÷ 9.81 = 2.1 s
B1: range would be less
B1: air resistance opposes motion so the horizontal velocity decreases (and the maximum height and time of flight are reduced)

questions.q: A 0.50 kg ball hits a wall at 6.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds at 4.0 m s⁻¹. What is the change in momentum?
questions.why: Δp = 0.50 × (4.0 − (−6.0)) = 5.0 N s, as the direction reverses.

questions.q: In a perfectly elastic collision, what is conserved besides momentum?
questions.why: Elastic means total kinetic energy is conserved; the relative speed of approach equals that of separation.

questions.q: Newton's second law states that resultant force equals…
o: the rate of change of momentum
questions.why: F = Δp/Δt, which becomes F = ma for constant mass.

questions.q: The pairs in Newton's third law act on…
questions.why: Third-law pairs are equal and opposite and act on different bodies.

questions.q: Which is a correct statement of Newton's second law?
o: The resultant force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum
Every force has an equal and opposite force
An object stays at rest unless acted on
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common mistake was 'force = mass × acceleration', which is not the law in full.

questions.q: Why does an astronaut feel weightless in an orbiting space station?
o: Earth gravity is zero at orbital altitude
Earth magnetic field shields the gravitational field
The astronaut and spacecraft are in free fall with the same gravitational acceleration
questions.why: Both the astronaut and the station accelerate towards Earth at g, so there is no normal reaction force between them.

long.q: A ball of mass 0.15 kg hits a wall at 20 m s⁻¹ and rebounds along the same line at 15 m s⁻¹. It is in contact with the wall for 0.050 s. Calculate the change in momentum of the ball and the average force on it.
scheme: C1: change in momentum = 0.15 × (15 − (−20))
A1: average force = 5.25 ÷ 0.050 = 105 N

long.q: A trolley A of mass 0.80 kg moving at 0.50 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary trolley B of mass 1.2 kg. The trolleys stick together. Calculate their common velocity after the collision and the loss of kinetic energy, and state whether the collision is elastic or inelastic.
scheme: C1: total momentum before = 0.80 × 0.50 = 0.40 N s = (0.80 + 1.2)v
C1: kinetic energy before = 0.100 J and after = ½ × 2.0 × 0.20² = 0.040 J
A1: loss = 0.060 J
B1: inelastic, because kinetic energy is not conserved

long.q: A skydiver jumps from a stationary balloon and falls vertically. Explain, in terms of the forces acting, why her acceleration decreases and she reaches a terminal velocity.
scheme: B1: weight acts downwards and is constant; air resistance (drag) acts upwards
B1: air resistance increases as her speed increases
B1: so the resultant (downward) force decreases and therefore her acceleration decreases (F = ma)
B1: at terminal velocity air resistance equals weight, the resultant force is zero and acceleration is zero

long.q: A lift of mass 600 kg carries passengers of total mass 240 kg. The lift accelerates upwards at 1.2 m s⁻². Calculate the tension in the lift cable and the force exerted by the floor on a passenger of mass 60 kg. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: C1: T − mg = ma with m = 840 kg
C1: for the passenger R − 60 × 9.81 = 60 × 1.2

long.q: A sphere P of mass 0.20 kg moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ makes a perfectly elastic head-on collision with a stationary sphere Q of mass 0.10 kg. Use conservation of momentum and the fact that, in an elastic collision, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation to calculate the velocities of P and Q after the collision.
scheme: A1: v_P = 1.0 m s⁻¹ in the original direction
A1: v_Q = 4.0 m s⁻¹ in the original direction
long.ans: P: 1.0 m s⁻¹; Q: 4.0 m s⁻¹

questions.q: For an object in equilibrium, which is true?
o: The resultant force is zero only
The resultant moment is zero only
Both the resultant force and the resultant moment are zero
questions.why: Equilibrium needs no resultant force and no resultant torque.

questions.q: What is upthrust on a submerged object equal to?
questions.why: Archimedes' principle; it comes from the pressure difference across the object (ρgV).

questions.q: The torque of a couple equals…
o: one force × the perpendicular distance between the forces
questions.why: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces produce a torque F × d.

questions.q: The centre of gravity of an object is the point where:
o: all the weight may be taken to act
the object balances only when it is symmetrical
questions.why: Examiners (2023): a common misconception was that all the weight actually acts there; it is where the weight is taken to act.

questions.q: A solid block of volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ is fully submerged in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. What is the upthrust on it? (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
questions.why: Upthrust = weight of water displaced = ρVg = 1000 × 2.0 × 10⁻³ × 9.81 ≈ 19.6 N. Leaving out g gives 2.0.

long.q: Calculate the pressure due to the water 3.0 m below the surface of a lake. The density of water is 1000 kg m⁻³. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: C1: p = ρgh

long.q: A uniform horizontal beam of length 4.0 m and weight 300 N is hinged to a wall at one end. It is held horizontal by a vertical rope attached 3.0 m from the hinge. A load of 200 N hangs from the free end of the beam. Calculate the tension in the rope and the vertical force exerted on the beam by the hinge.
scheme: C1: taking moments about the hinge: T × 3.0 = 300 × 2.0 + 200 × 4.0
C1: vertical forces balance: hinge force + T = 500 N
A1: hinge force = 33 N upwards

long.q: A block of wood of volume 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and density 650 kg m⁻³ is held completely under water by a string tied to the bottom of a tank. The density of water is 1000 kg m⁻³. Explain why there is an upthrust on the block, then calculate the upthrust and the tension in the string. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: B1: pressure increases with depth, so the pressure on the lower face is greater than on the upper face, giving a net upward force
C1: upthrust = weight of water displaced = ρVg = 1000 × 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 9.81
A1: upthrust = 2.45 N
C1: weight of block = 650 × 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 9.81 = 1.59 N

long.q: Define the torque of a couple. A driver turns a steering wheel of diameter 0.38 m by applying two equal and opposite forces of 25 N, each tangential to the rim, at opposite ends of a diameter. Calculate the torque applied.
scheme: B1: torque of a couple = one of the forces × the perpendicular distance between the lines of action of the two forces
C1: torque = 25 × 0.38

long.q: State the two conditions for a body to be in equilibrium. A picture of weight 12 N hangs from a single nail by a string; the two sections of string each make an angle of 25° with the horizontal. Calculate the tension in the string, and explain why the tension would be greater if a shorter string were used.
scheme: B1: the resultant force on the body is zero
B1: the resultant torque (moment) about any point is zero
C1: vertically: 2T sin 25° = 12
B1: a shorter string makes a smaller angle with the horizontal, so sin θ is smaller and T must be larger to supply the same vertical component

questions.q: A motor lifts a 20 kg load 3.0 m in 4.0 s. What is its useful power output? (g = 9.81)
Power can also be written as…
questions.why: P = W/t = F × (s/t) = Fv.

questions.q: A machine has 600 J input and 450 J useful output. Its efficiency is…
What does the area under a force–extension graph represent for a spring obeying Hooke's law?
o: The elastic potential energy stored in the spring
The work done per unit volume
questions.why: Work done W = ∫ F dx, which equals the area under the force–extension curve (½kx²).

questions.q: A car of mass 1200 kg speeds up from 10 m s⁻¹ to 20 m s⁻¹. How much work is done by the resultant force on it?
questions.why: Work done by the resultant force = change in kinetic energy = ½ × 1200 × (20² − 10²) = 600 × 300 = 1.8 × 10⁵ J.

long.q: A climber of mass 60 kg climbs a vertical height of 25 m in 50 s. Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy and the average useful power. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: C1: ΔEp = mgΔh
A1: power = 294 W

long.q: Show that the power P needed to move an object at constant velocity v against a constant force F is given by P = Fv. An electric motor lifts a load of mass 40 kg vertically at a constant speed of 0.50 m s⁻¹. The input power to the motor is 300 W. Calculate the efficiency of the motor. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: M1: P = work done ÷ time = (F × distance) ÷ time
A1: distance ÷ time = v, so P = Fv
C1: useful output power = mgv = 40 × 9.81 × 0.50 = 196 W
C1: efficiency = useful output power ÷ input power

long.q: A roller-coaster car of mass 500 kg starts from rest at the top of a track 30 m above its lowest point. It reaches the lowest point with a speed of 22 m s⁻¹ after travelling 120 m along the track. Calculate the work done against resistive forces and the average resistive force. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: C1: loss of gravitational potential energy = 500 × 9.81 × 30 = 1.47 × 10⁵ J
C1: gain of kinetic energy = ½ × 500 × 22² = 1.21 × 10⁵ J
A1: work done against resistive forces = 2.6 × 10⁴ J
A1: average resistive force = 2.6 × 10⁴ ÷ 120 = 220 N

long.q: A car has a maximum output power of 60 kW. On a level road its top speed is 50 m s⁻¹. Calculate the total resistive force at top speed. Then explain why, when the car accelerates at constant output power, its acceleration decreases as its speed increases.
scheme: C1: at top speed driving force = resistive force and P = Fv
B1: at constant power the driving force (P ÷ v) decreases as speed increases
B1: resistive forces increase with speed, so the resultant force and hence the acceleration decrease

long.q: Use the equations of uniformly accelerated motion to show that the kinetic energy of an object of mass m moving at speed v is ½mv².
scheme: M1: work done by a constant resultant force F accelerating the mass from rest through distance s is W = Fs, with F = ma
M1: from v² = u² + 2as with u = 0, as = v²/2
A1: W = mas = ½mv², which equals the kinetic energy gained

questions.q: Young modulus is defined as…
questions.why: E = stress/strain, in Pa.

questions.q: What does the area under a force–extension graph (within the limit of proportionality) represent?
questions.why: Work done stretching it = ½Fx.

questions.q: Plastic deformation means the material…
o: does not return to its original shape when the load is removed
questions.why: Beyond the elastic limit, the deformation is permanent.

questions.q: A wire is stretched so that its length increases. Ignoring temperature, what happens to its resistance?
o: It decreases because the area increases
It increases only because the length increases
It increases because the length increases and the area decreases
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many ignored the change in cross-sectional area when the wire is stretched.

questions.q: Wires A and B are made of the same metal. B is twice as long as A and has twice the diameter. Each carries the same load. What is (extension of B) ÷ (extension of A)?
questions.why: Extension = FL/(AE). Doubling the diameter makes the area 4 times larger, so B's extension is 2/4 = 0.5 of A's.

long.q: A wire of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 0.40 mm² extends by 1.2 mm when a load of 50 N hangs from it. Calculate the Young modulus of the wire.
scheme: C1: E = stress ÷ strain

long.q: A spring obeys Hooke's law and extends by 6.0 cm when a load of 3.0 N hangs from it. Calculate the spring constant and the elastic potential energy stored. Two of these springs are then joined end to end (in series) and the same 3.0 N load is hung from them. State the total extension and calculate the total elastic potential energy stored.
scheme: B1: each spring extends 6.0 cm, total extension 12 cm

long.q: Distinguish between elastic deformation and plastic deformation of a material. A metal wire is loaded beyond its elastic limit and then unloaded. Explain what the area between the loading and unloading lines of its force–extension graph represents.
scheme: B1: elastic deformation: the material returns to its original shape and size when the load is removed
B1: plastic deformation: the material does not return to its original shape; there is a permanent extension
B1: the area under a force–extension graph represents work done (energy)
B1: the area between the lines is the energy not recovered on unloading, dissipated (as thermal energy) in permanently deforming the wire

long.q: Describe how you would determine the Young modulus of the metal of a long thin wire in a school laboratory. Include the measurements you would make, the instruments used and how you would calculate the result.
scheme: B1: fix one end of the wire and hang loads from the other (e.g. over a pulley), with a marker or a reference wire alongside
B1: measure the original length with a metre rule (or tape) from the fixed end to the marker
B1: measure the diameter with a micrometer at several places and average, to find the cross-sectional area πd²/4
B1: add loads in steps and measure the extension each time with a vernier scale or travelling microscope
B1: plot a graph of force against extension and find the gradient in the linear region
B1: Young modulus = gradient × original length ÷ cross-sectional area

long.q: Two wires A and B are made of the same metal. Wire B is twice as long as wire A and has twice the diameter. The same load is hung from each wire and both obey Hooke's law. Determine the ratio extension of B ÷ extension of A, and the ratio of the elastic strain energy stored in B to that stored in A.
scheme: C1: extension = FL ÷ (AE), and B has twice the length and four times the cross-sectional area
A1: extension ratio = 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5
B1: strain energy = ½Fx with the same F, so energy ratio = 0.5

questions.q: Intensity of a wave is proportional to…
questions.why: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared: I ∝ A².

questions.q: A source moves towards a stationary observer. The observed frequency is…
questions.why: Doppler effect: wavefronts bunch up, so the frequency observed is higher.

questions.q: Which waves can be polarised?
questions.why: Polarisation restricts oscillation to one plane, which needs transverse oscillations.

questions.q: Unpolarised light passes through a polariser, then an analyser at 60°. What fraction of the light after the polariser gets through? (Malus's law)
questions.why: I = I₀ cos²60° = 0.25 I₀.

questions.q: A wave has wavelength 2.1 cm. In which region of the electromagnetic spectrum is it?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some thought 2.1 cm was a radio wave. Microwaves run from about 1 mm to 30 cm.

questions.q: What is true for all electromagnetic waves travelling through a vacuum?
o: They have the same speed (3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.why: All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light c in free space, though frequencies and wavelengths vary.

long.q: The graph shows the displacement of the particles of a wave against distance at one instant. The frequency of the wave is 50 Hz. Use the graph to find the amplitude and the wavelength, and calculate the speed of the wave.
scheme: B1: amplitude = 3.0 mm
B1: wavelength = 0.40 m
A1: v = fλ = 20 m s⁻¹

long.q: A car horn emits sound of frequency 800 Hz. The car moves at a constant speed of 30 m s⁻¹ directly towards a stationary observer, then directly away. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Calculate the frequency heard by the observer as the car approaches and as it recedes.
scheme: C1: f_o = f_s v ÷ (v − v_s) for an approaching source
C1: f_o = f_s v ÷ (v + v_s) for a receding source

long.q: Define the intensity of a wave. The amplitude of a wave of intensity 4.0 W m⁻² is reduced to 60% of its original value. Calculate the new intensity.
scheme: B1: intensity = power transmitted per unit area (normal to the direction of travel of the wave)
C1: intensity ∝ amplitude², so new intensity = 4.0 × 0.60²
A1: 1.4 W m⁻²

long.q: Unpolarised light of intensity 40 W m⁻² passes through a polarising filter and then through a second polarising filter whose transmission axis is at 60° to that of the first. Calculate the intensity of the light leaving each filter, and explain why sound waves cannot be polarised.
scheme: B1: intensity after the first filter = 40 ÷ 2 = 20 W m⁻²
C1: Malus's law I = I₀ cos² θ = 20 × cos² 60°
A1: 5.0 W m⁻²
B1: sound is a longitudinal wave; polarisation needs oscillations perpendicular to the direction of travel (transverse waves only)

long.q: A sound wave of frequency 250 Hz travels through air at 340 m s⁻¹. Describe the motion of the air particles as the wave passes, then calculate the phase difference between the oscillations of two particles 0.34 m apart along the direction of travel.
scheme: B1: particles oscillate about fixed positions parallel to the direction of energy transfer, forming compressions and rarefactions
C1: phase difference = (0.34 ÷ 1.36) × 360°

questions.q: In a stationary wave, the distance between adjacent nodes is…
questions.why: Nodes are half a wavelength apart.

questions.q: In Young's double-slit experiment, fringe spacing x = λD/a. What happens if the slit separation a is halved?
questions.why: x is inversely proportional to a.

questions.q: A diffraction grating has 500 lines per mm. What is the line spacing d?
For a stable interference pattern, the sources must be…
questions.why: Coherent sources have a constant phase difference.

questions.q: Two waves meet. What is needed for them to superpose?
o: They must be of the same type and meet at a point
They must have the same frequency
They must travel in opposite directions
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many confused the condition for superposition with those for stationary waves or a stable interference pattern.

questions.q: Two coherent light sources emit waves that arrive at a point in phase with equal amplitude A. What is the resultant intensity compared to one source alone?
o: 4 times the intensity of one source
questions.why: Amplitudes add constructively: A_res = 2A. Since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, I_res ∝ (2A)² = 4A².

long.q: In a double-slit experiment the slits are 0.50 mm apart and the screen is 2.0 m away. Light of wavelength 600 nm is used. Calculate the fringe separation.
scheme: C1: x = λD ÷ a

long.q: Light of wavelength 589 nm is incident normally on a diffraction grating with 500 lines per millimetre. Calculate the angle of the first-order maximum and the highest order that can be observed.
scheme: A1: highest order = 3

long.q: A string fixed at both ends is 0.90 m long. When vibrated at 120 Hz it forms a stationary wave with three loops (antinodes). Calculate the wavelength and the speed of waves on the string, and the frequency of the fundamental mode. State two ways in which a stationary wave differs from a progressive wave.
scheme: C1: three loops = 1.5λ = 0.90 m, λ = 0.60 m
A1: fundamental λ = 1.80 m, f = 72 ÷ 1.80 = 40 Hz
B1: stationary waves have nodes and antinodes (amplitude varies with position); progressive waves have the same amplitude everywhere
B1: stationary waves do not transfer energy, or all points between adjacent nodes oscillate in phase

long.q: Explain what is meant by coherent sources, and state the conditions needed to observe a clear two-source interference pattern. Suggest why light from two separate filament lamps does not produce an observable interference pattern.
scheme: B1: coherent sources have a constant phase difference
B1: sources must have the same frequency (wavelength) and be coherent
B1: waves must have similar amplitudes (and, if transverse, the same polarisation), with source separation small compared with the distance to the screen
B1: the two lamps emit light in random, independent bursts, so their phase difference changes constantly and the pattern changes too quickly to see

long.q: Two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator emit sound in phase. A point P is 4.20 m from one loudspeaker and 4.88 m from the other. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Determine whether the sound at P is loud or quiet when the frequency is 1000 Hz, and when it is 1250 Hz. Explain your answers.
scheme: C1: path difference = 0.68 m; at 1000 Hz λ = 0.34 m
A1: path difference = 2λ, so the waves arrive in phase: constructive interference, loud
A1: path difference = 2.5λ, so the waves arrive in antiphase: destructive interference, quiet
long.ans: loud at 1000 Hz; quiet at 1250 Hz

questions.q: A wire of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m² has resistivity 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What is its resistance?
In I = Anvq, what is v?
o: The mean drift velocity of the charge carriers
questions.why: n is the number density, A the area, q the charge, v the drift velocity.

questions.q: Power dissipated in a resistor can be written as…
questions.why: P = VI = I²R = V²/R.

questions.q: Two wires of the same metal are connected in series. The second has half the cross-sectional area of the first. What is (drift velocity in the second) ÷ (drift velocity in the first)?
questions.why: I = Anvq, and I, n and q are the same in both, so v ∝ 1/A. Halving A doubles the drift velocity.

questions.q: A heater is rated 2.0 kW at 230 V. What is its resistance when working normally?
questions.why: P = V²/R, so R = 230²/2000 ≈ 26 Ω. 8.7 is the current in amperes, not the resistance.

long.q: A wire of length 1.5 m and diameter 0.40 mm is made of metal of resistivity 4.9 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m. Calculate its resistance.
scheme: C1: R = ρL ÷ A

long.q: A current of 0.25 A flows in a lamp for 3.0 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes through the lamp and the number of electrons this represents. (e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
scheme: A1: number of electrons = 45 ÷ 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 2.8 × 10²⁰

long.q: A copper wire has a cross-sectional area of 1.0 mm² and carries a current of 2.0 A. The number density of free electrons in copper is 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³. Calculate the average drift speed of the electrons, and explain how the drift speed changes where the wire becomes thinner. (e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
scheme: C1: I = Anvq so v = I ÷ (Anq)
B1: the current is the same throughout the wire, so where A is smaller the drift speed is greater

long.q: Describe and explain the shape of the current–voltage (I–V) characteristic of a filament lamp, for both positive and negative potential differences.
scheme: B1: graph passes through the origin and is approximately straight at small currents
B1: gradient decreases as the potential difference increases (curve flattens), and the graph has the same shape for negative values (symmetrical)
B1: resistance increases as the current increases because the temperature of the filament rises
B1: the lattice ions vibrate more, so the electrons collide with them more often

long.q: An electric kettle is rated at 2.4 kW when connected to a 230 V supply. Calculate the current in the heating element, its resistance, and the energy transferred in 3.0 minutes.
scheme: B1: R = V² ÷ P = 22 Ω

questions.q: Kirchhoff's first law is a consequence of conservation of…
questions.why: Current into a junction equals current out: charge is conserved.

questions.q: A cell of e.m.f. 6.0 V and internal resistance 1.0 Ω is connected to a 5.0 Ω resistor. What is the current?
In a potential divider of 2 kΩ (top) and 8 kΩ (bottom) across 10 V, what is the output across the 8 kΩ?
A battery of e.m.f. 9.6 V and negligible internal resistance is in series with two resistors. The p.d. across one is 6.0 V. What is the p.d. across the other, of resistance 5800 Ω?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates assumed 6.0 V or 9.6 V. In series the p.d.s add to the e.m.f.: 9.6 − 6.0 = 3.6 V.

questions.q: Two 6.0 Ω resistors in parallel are connected in series with a 3.0 Ω resistor. What is the total resistance?
questions.why: The parallel pair gives 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6, so R = 3.0 Ω; adding the 3.0 Ω in series gives 6.0 Ω.

long.q: In the circuit shown, the battery has an e.m.f. of 12 V and negligible internal resistance. Calculate the current from the battery and the potential difference across the 3.0 Ω resistor.
scheme: C1: the parallel pair is 2.0 Ω
C1: total resistance 6.0 Ω
A1: current = 2.0 A
A1: p.d. across the 3.0 Ω resistor = 4.0 V

long.q: A battery of e.m.f. 9.0 V is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor. The potential difference across the resistor is 8.0 V. Explain why this is less than the e.m.f., then calculate the internal resistance of the battery and the power dissipated in it.
scheme: B1: some energy per unit charge is transferred in the internal resistance of the battery (lost volts)
C1: lost volts = 9.0 − 8.0 = 1.0 V
A1: power = I²r = 2.0 W

long.q: A potential divider consists of a fixed resistor of 2.0 kΩ in series with a negative temperature coefficient (NTC) thermistor, connected across a 12 V supply of negligible internal resistance. The output is taken across the thermistor. At 20 °C the thermistor's resistance is 3.0 kΩ. Calculate the output voltage at 20 °C, and explain how the output voltage changes as the temperature rises.
scheme: B1: as temperature rises the resistance of the thermistor decreases
B1: the thermistor takes a smaller share of the 12 V, so the output voltage decreases

long.q: State Kirchhoff's first law and Kirchhoff's second law, and state the quantity whose conservation each law expresses.
scheme: B1: first law: the sum of the currents into a junction equals the sum of the currents out of it
B1: first law is a consequence of conservation of charge
B1: second law: around any closed loop the sum of the e.m.f.s equals the sum of the potential differences
B1: second law is a consequence of conservation of energy

long.q: A potentiometer consists of a uniform resistance wire 1.00 m long connected across a driver cell of e.m.f. 2.0 V and negligible internal resistance. A test cell in series with a galvanometer is connected between one end of the wire and a sliding contact, with like terminals of the two cells connected together. The galvanometer reads zero when the sliding contact is 0.72 m from that end. Calculate the e.m.f. of the test cell, and explain why this method measures the e.m.f. rather than the terminal potential difference.
scheme: C1: potential difference per unit length = 2.0 V m⁻¹
B1: at balance there is no current in the test cell, so there is no potential difference across its internal resistance

questions.q: What is the quark composition of a proton?
questions.why: Two up (+2/3 each) and one down (−1/3): total charge +1.

questions.q: In β⁻ decay, a down quark changes into…
questions.why: d → u + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ.

questions.q: Which are leptons?
questions.why: Leptons are fundamental particles that don't feel the strong force.

questions.q: Which particles are found in the nucleus?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): some weaker candidates thought there are electrons in the nucleus.

questions.q: A meson consists of an up quark and an anti-down quark (u d̄). What is its charge?
questions.why: u has charge +⅔e and d has −⅓e, so d̄ has +⅓e. The total is +⅔e + ⅓e = +e.

long.q: A proton is made of up (u) and down (d) quarks. State its quark composition and show that its charge is +e.
scheme: B1: uud

long.q: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, alpha particles were directed at a thin gold foil. Describe the observations and state what each one shows about the structure of the atom.
scheme: B1: most alpha particles passed straight through, so the atom is mostly empty space
B1: some were deflected through small angles and a very few through large angles (more than 90°)
B1: so the nucleus is very small compared with the atom and is positively charged
B1: most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in the nucleus

long.q: Write an equation, in terms of particles, for the β⁻ decay of a neutron, and state the change in quark composition that occurs. Explain why the β⁻ particles emitted by a given nuclide have a range of kinetic energies.
scheme: B1: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ (electron antineutrino)
B1: udd → uud, i.e. a down quark changes to an up quark
B1: the energy released in each decay is shared between the β⁻ particle and the antineutrino
B1: the share varies from decay to decay, so the β⁻ particles have a continuous spread of energies up to a maximum

long.q: A nucleus of uranium-238 (proton number 92) decays by emitting an α particle. The product then undergoes two successive β⁻ decays. Determine the nucleon number and proton number of the final nucleus, and state what it has in common with the original nucleus.
scheme: B1: α decay: nucleon number 234, proton number 90
B1: after two β⁻ decays: nucleon number 234, proton number 92
B1: same proton number, so it is an isotope of uranium (the same element)

long.q: Classify each of the following as a hadron or a lepton, and state whether each hadron is a baryon or a meson: neutron, electron, π⁺ meson. The π⁺ has quark composition u d̄; show that its charge is +e, and state what is meant by an antiparticle.
scheme: B1: neutron: hadron, baryon; electron: lepton
B1: π⁺: hadron, meson
B1: charge = (+⅔ e) + (+⅓ e) = +e, since the anti-down quark has charge +⅓ e
B1: an antiparticle has the same mass as its particle but opposite charge (and other opposite quantum numbers)

questions.q: An object moves in a circle of radius 2.0 m at 4.0 m s⁻¹. What is its centripetal acceleration?
Angular speed ω is related to period T by…
questions.why: One revolution is 2π radians in time T.

questions.q: A body moves at constant speed in a circle. Its acceleration is:
o: Towards the centre, with constant magnitude
questions.why: The direction of velocity changes, so there is a centripetal acceleration v²/r.

questions.q: A car of mass m travels over the crest of a curved hill of radius r at speed v. What is the normal reaction force on the car?
questions.why: Resultant force towards the centre of the curvature is mg − N = mv²/r, so N = mg − mv²/r.

questions.q: A wheel turns at 1200 revolutions per minute. What is its angular speed?
questions.why: 1200 rev/min = 20 rev/s, and each revolution is 2π rad, so ω = 2π × 20 ≈ 126 rad s⁻¹.

long.q: A car of mass 900 kg travels at a constant speed of 15 m s⁻¹ round a horizontal bend of radius 50 m. Calculate the centripetal force required.
scheme: C1: F = mv²/r

long.q: Define the radian. A wheel of radius 0.30 m rotates at 1200 revolutions per minute. Calculate its angular speed and the linear speed of a point on its rim.
scheme: B1: one radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius
A1: 126 rad s⁻¹
A1: v = ωr = 37.7 m s⁻¹

long.q: A ball of mass 0.25 kg on a string is whirled in a vertical circle of radius 0.80 m. At the top of the circle its speed is 4.0 m s⁻¹. Calculate the tension in the string at the top, and the minimum speed at the top for the string to stay taut. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: M1: at the top, T + mg = mv²/r
M1: minimum speed when T = 0, so mg = mv²/r and v = √(gr)
A1: v = 2.8 m s⁻¹

long.q: An object moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Explain why it is accelerating, state the direction of the resultant force on it, and explain why this force does no work on the object.
scheme: B1: its direction of motion is continually changing, so its velocity changes and it accelerates
B1: the resultant (centripetal) force is directed towards the centre of the circle
B1: the force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so there is no displacement in the direction of the force and no work is done (speed and kinetic energy stay constant)

long.q: A small mass of 0.20 kg on a string of length 0.50 m moves in a horizontal circle so that the string makes a constant angle of 30° with the vertical (a conical pendulum). Calculate the tension in the string, the angular speed of the mass and the period of its motion. (g = 9.81 m s⁻²)
scheme: C1: vertically T cos 30° = mg
C1: horizontally T sin 30° = mω²r with r = 0.50 sin 30° = 0.25 m
A1: ω = 4.76 rad s⁻¹
A1: period = 2π ÷ ω = 1.32 s

questions.q: If the distance between two masses doubles, the gravitational force becomes…
questions.why: F = GMm/r², an inverse-square law.

questions.q: A geostationary satellite has an orbital period of…
questions.why: It orbits above the equator, in the same direction as Earth's rotation, once every 24 hours.

questions.q: Gravitational potential at a point is…
questions.why: φ = −GM/r: work must be done to move a mass to infinity.

questions.q: Why is gravitational potential in a field always defined as negative?
o: Gravity repels objects at short distances
Energy cannot have positive values in physics
Gravitational force is attractive and potential is defined as zero at infinity
Mass is mathematically negative in field equations
questions.why: Work is done by the attractive field bringing mass from infinity, so potential is zero at infinity and negative everywhere else.

questions.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit of radius r at speed v. At what speed would it move in a circular orbit of radius 4r about the same planet?
questions.why: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r). Multiplying r by 4 divides v by 2.

long.q: Show that the orbital period T of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r about a planet of mass M satisfies T² = 4π²r³/(GM).
scheme: M1: GMm/r² = mv²/r (gravity provides centripetal force)
M1: v = 2πr/T
A1: substitution and rearrangement to T² = 4π²r³/(GM)

long.q: State three features of the orbit of a geostationary satellite. Calculate the radius of a geostationary orbit about the Earth. (Mass of Earth = 5.98 × 10²⁴ kg, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
scheme: B1: period of 24 hours (equal to Earth's rotation period) and orbit directly above the equator
B1: moves in the same direction as the Earth rotates (west to east), so stays above the same point
C1: GMm/r² = mω²r with ω = 2π ÷ (24 × 3600), so r³ = GMT²/(4π²)

long.q: Explain why the gravitational potential near a planet is negative. A satellite of mass 1200 kg is lifted from the Earth's surface into an orbit 600 km above the surface. Calculate the increase in its gravitational potential energy. (Mass of Earth = 5.98 × 10²⁴ kg, radius of Earth = 6.37 × 10⁶ m, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
scheme: B1: potential is zero at infinity; gravitational forces are attractive, so work is done by the field as a mass moves in from infinity and the potential is less than zero
M1: ΔEp = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂)

long.q: An astronaut in a spacecraft orbiting the Earth feels weightless, even though the Earth's gravitational field strength at that height is not zero. Explain why.
scheme: B1: the gravitational force on the astronaut (and spacecraft) provides the centripetal force for the circular orbit
B1: astronaut and spacecraft are both in free fall with the same acceleration
B1: so there is no contact (normal) force between the astronaut and the floor, which is what is felt as weight

long.q: The mass of the Earth is 81 times the mass of the Moon and their centres are 3.84 × 10⁸ m apart. Calculate the distance from the centre of the Earth, along the line joining the centres, at which the resultant gravitational field strength due to the Earth and Moon is zero.
scheme: M1: GM_E/x² = GM_M/(d − x)²

questions.q: What is 27 °C in kelvin?
How much energy melts 0.20 kg of ice at 0 °C? (specific latent heat of fusion 3.3 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)
Specific latent heat of fusion is the energy needed to:
o: Change unit mass from solid to liquid with no change in temperature
questions.why: Learn definitions exactly: 'unit mass' and 'no change in temperature' both matter.

questions.q: How much energy is needed to heat 0.50 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C? (specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹)
questions.why: E = mcΔθ = 0.50 × 4200 × 60 = 1.26 × 10⁵ J. Using 80 °C instead of the change of 60 K gives 1.68 × 10⁵ J.

questions.q: Two objects in contact are in thermal equilibrium. Which statement must be true?
o: They have the same internal energy
They have the same specific heat capacity
No energy at all passes between them
They are at the same temperature, so there is no net transfer of thermal energy between them
questions.why: Thermal equilibrium means equal temperature, so there is no net energy flow. Energy can still pass both ways at equal rates, and the internal energies can differ.

long.q: Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.25 kg of ice at 0 °C. (Specific latent heat of fusion = 3.3 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)
scheme: C1: E = mL

long.q: An electric heater of power 50 W is placed in an aluminium block of mass 0.80 kg. After 300 s the temperature of the block has risen from 20.0 °C to 40.5 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium given by these results, and explain whether the true value is likely to be higher or lower.
scheme: C1: energy supplied = Pt = 50 × 300 = 1.5 × 10⁴ J
A1: 910 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹
B1: true value is lower, because some energy is lost to the surroundings so less than 1.5 × 10⁴ J actually heated the block

long.q: Explain what is meant by (a) two objects being in thermal equilibrium, and (b) absolute zero. Convert a temperature of −40 °C to the thermodynamic (kelvin) scale.
scheme: B1: thermal equilibrium: there is no net transfer of thermal energy between them, because they are at the same temperature
B1: absolute zero: the temperature at which a substance has minimum internal energy (0 K)

long.q: 0.20 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 0.30 kg of water at 20 °C in an insulated container of negligible heat capacity. Calculate the final temperature of the mixture.
scheme: M1: thermal energy lost by hot water = thermal energy gained by cold water

long.q: Explain, in terms of molecules, why the temperature of a substance stays constant while it melts, and why the specific latent heat of vaporisation of water is much greater than its specific latent heat of fusion.
scheme: B1: while melting, the energy supplied increases the potential energy of the molecules (breaking bonds), not their kinetic energy, so temperature is constant
B1: during melting the molecules separate only slightly (some bonds broken)
B1: during vaporisation the molecules are separated completely to large distances (all bonds broken), needing much more energy
B1: during vaporisation work is also done pushing back the atmosphere as the volume increases greatly

questions.q: The mean kinetic energy of a molecule in an ideal gas is proportional to…
questions.why: ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT.

questions.q: For an ideal gas, pV = …
questions.why: The ideal gas equation, with n in moles.

questions.q: The mean kinetic energy of the molecules of an ideal gas is proportional to:
questions.why: Mean E_k = (3/2)kT.

questions.q: A fixed mass of ideal gas at constant volume is heated from 27 °C to 327 °C. By what factor does its pressure change?
questions.why: At constant volume p ∝ T in kelvin: 300 K to 600 K doubles the pressure. Using °C values gives the wrong factor of about 12.

questions.q: The thermodynamic temperature of an ideal gas is quadrupled. What happens to the root-mean-square speed of its molecules?
o: It increases by a factor of √2
It increases by a factor of 16
questions.why: ½m⟨c²⟩ = (3/2)kT, so ⟨c²⟩ ∝ T and c_rms ∝ √T. Quadrupling T doubles c_rms.

long.q: A gas cylinder of volume 0.020 m³ contains an ideal gas at 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and 300 K. Calculate the number of moles of gas. (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
scheme: C1: n = pV/(RT)
A1: = 1.6 mol

long.q: Calculate the mean kinetic energy of a molecule of nitrogen gas at 300 K and the root-mean-square speed of the molecules. (Molar mass of nitrogen = 0.028 kg mol⁻¹, k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
scheme: C1: mean kinetic energy = (3/2)kT = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 300
C1: mass of one molecule = 0.028 ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, and ½m⟨c²⟩ = 6.2 × 10⁻²¹ J
A1: c_rms = 517 m s⁻¹

long.q: State four assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.
scheme: B1: molecules are in constant random motion
B1: collisions of molecules with each other and with the walls are elastic
B1: the volume of the molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the container
B1: there are no intermolecular forces except during collisions, and the time of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions

long.q: Explain, in terms of the motion of its molecules, how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container, and why the pressure increases when the gas is heated at constant volume.
scheme: B1: molecules collide with the walls and rebound, so their momentum changes
B1: the wall exerts a force on each molecule, so by Newton's third law the molecules exert a force on the wall; pressure is the total force per unit area
B1: when heated, the mean kinetic energy (mean speed) of the molecules increases
B1: so the change in momentum per collision and the number of collisions per unit time both increase, increasing the force and the pressure

long.q: A fixed mass of ideal gas has a pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, a volume of 2.4 × 10⁻³ m³ and a temperature of 290 K. It is compressed to a volume of 0.80 × 10⁻³ m³ and its temperature rises to 340 K. Calculate the new pressure.
scheme: M1: p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂

questions.q: The first law of thermodynamics is ΔU = q + W. W is…
questions.why: In the Cambridge convention, W is work done on the system.

questions.q: For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on…
questions.why: There are no intermolecular forces, so internal energy is all kinetic, set by temperature.

questions.q: In the first law, ΔU = q + W. What is W?
o: The work done on the system
The work done by the system
questions.why: Compressing a gas does work on it, so W is positive.

questions.q: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa from 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 5.0 × 10⁻³ m³ while 500 J of heat is supplied to it. What is the change in its internal energy?
questions.why: Work done on the gas W = −pΔV = −300 J. ΔU = q + W = 500 − 300 = +200 J.

questions.q: An ideal gas is compressed so quickly that no heat enters or leaves it. What happens to its temperature?
o: It stays the same, because q = 0
It falls, because the gas does work
It rises, because heat is supplied
It rises, because the work done on the gas increases its internal energy
questions.why: With q = 0, ΔU = W, and W is positive in a compression. The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, so the temperature rises.

long.q: State what is meant by the internal energy of a system, and state the first law of thermodynamics in terms of the increase in internal energy, the heating of the system and the work done on the system.
scheme: B1: internal energy = sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the molecules of the system
B1: ΔU = q + W
B1: ΔU is the increase in internal energy, q is the energy transferred to the system by heating and W is the work done on the system

long.q: A gas at a constant pressure of 1.5 × 10⁵ Pa expands from a volume of 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ to 3.2 × 10⁻³ m³ while 450 J of thermal energy is supplied to it. Calculate the work done by the gas and the change in its internal energy, and state what happens to its temperature.
scheme: C1: work done by gas = pΔV = 1.5 × 10⁵ × 1.2 × 10⁻³
A1: 180 J (so work done on the gas W = −180 J)
B1: internal energy increases, so the temperature rises

long.q: Explain why the internal energy of an ideal gas consists only of the kinetic energy of its molecules, and why, for a fixed mass of ideal gas, the internal energy is proportional to the thermodynamic temperature.
scheme: B1: there are no intermolecular forces in an ideal gas
B1: so the molecules have no potential energy and the internal energy is the total random kinetic energy
B1: the mean kinetic energy of a molecule is (3/2)kT, so the total kinetic energy (with N fixed) is proportional to T

long.q: A gas is taken through a complete cycle of changes and returns to its original pressure, volume and temperature. During the cycle 600 J of thermal energy is supplied to the gas and 420 J of thermal energy is transferred from it. Explain why the change in internal energy over the cycle is zero, and calculate the net work done by the gas.
scheme: B1: internal energy depends only on the state of the gas (its temperature), which is the same at the end as at the start
C1: net q = 600 − 420 = 180 J and ΔU = 0 so W = −180 J
A1: net work done by the gas = 180 J

long.q: 0.050 mol of an ideal monatomic gas is compressed so quickly that no thermal energy is transferred to or from it. 75 J of work is done on the gas. State the change in internal energy of the gas and calculate the rise in its temperature. (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
scheme: B1: q = 0, so ΔU = W = +75 J
M1: internal energy U = (3/2)nRT (number of molecules × (3/2)kT)

questions.q: In simple harmonic motion, acceleration is…
o: proportional to displacement and opposite in direction
questions.why: Defining equation of SHM: a = −ω²x.

questions.q: At what point of an SHM is the speed greatest?
questions.why: All the energy is kinetic at x = 0.

questions.q: What is resonance?
o: A large amplitude when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency
questions.why: Maximum energy transfer happens when the frequencies match.

questions.q: A particle moves with simple harmonic motion given by x = 0.050 sin(10t), with x in metres and t in seconds. What is its maximum acceleration?
questions.why: a_max = ω²x₀ = 10² × 0.050 = 5.0 m s⁻². ωx₀ = 0.50 is the maximum speed, not acceleration.

questions.q: A mass on a spring oscillates with simple harmonic motion of period 0.50 s. What is its angular frequency?
questions.why: ω = 2π/T = 2π ÷ 0.50 ≈ 12.6 rad s⁻¹ (13 to 2 s.f.). 2.0 is the frequency in Hz, not the angular frequency.

long.q: A mass on a spring oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 3.0 cm and frequency 2.0 Hz. Calculate its maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
scheme: C1: ω = 2πf = 4π rad s⁻¹ (12.6)
A1: v_max = ωx₀ = 0.38 m s⁻¹
A1: a_max = ω²x₀ = 4.7 m s⁻²

long.q: Define simple harmonic motion. The acceleration a of an oscillator is related to its displacement x by a = −ω²x. Explain the significance of the negative sign.
scheme: B1: acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point (the equilibrium position)
B1: and is always directed towards that fixed point
B1: the negative sign shows that the acceleration is always in the opposite direction to the displacement

long.q: Describe and explain the phenomenon of resonance. State and explain how increasing the damping of an oscillating system affects the graph of its amplitude against driving frequency.
scheme: B1: resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of the system
B1: the amplitude of oscillation is then a maximum, because energy is transferred to the system most efficiently
B1: increasing damping reduces the amplitude at all frequencies and makes the peak flatter (broader)
B1: the frequency of the peak becomes slightly lower than the natural frequency

long.q: A mass of 0.40 kg on a spring of spring constant 160 N m⁻¹ oscillates with simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.050 m. Show that the angular frequency is 20 rad s⁻¹, then calculate the total energy of the oscillation and the speed of the mass when its displacement is 0.030 m.
scheme: M1: F = −kx so a = −(k/m)x and ω² = k/m
C1: E = ½mω²x₀² = ½ × 0.40 × 20² × 0.050²

long.q: Plan an experiment to investigate how the period T of vertical oscillations of a mass on a spring depends on the mass m. It is suggested that T is proportional to √m. Describe the procedure, the measurements and how you would use a graph to test the suggestion. Include any precautions for accuracy and safety.
scheme: B1: independent variable m, dependent variable T; keep the same spring throughout
B1: measure m using a top-pan balance (or use slotted masses of known value)
B1: displace the mass a small distance vertically and release; keep the amplitude small and the same each time
B1: use a stopwatch to time at least 10 oscillations and divide by the number of oscillations
B1: use a fiducial marker at the equilibrium position to start and stop timing; repeat timings and average
B1: plot a graph of T² against m (or lg T against lg m)
B1: the suggestion is supported if the T² against m graph is a straight line through the origin (or the log graph has gradient 0.5)
B1: safety: clamp the stand firmly / use a G-clamp and place a tray of sand or soft material below in case the mass falls

questions.q: The electric field between parallel plates 0.020 m apart with 400 V across them is…
Coulomb's law: halving the distance between two charges makes the force…
questions.why: Coulomb's law is an inverse-square law: F ∝ 1/r².

questions.q: Electric field strength is:
o: The force per unit positive charge
questions.why: Units N C⁻¹ (= V m⁻¹).

questions.q: What is the electric field strength 0.30 m from a point charge of +2.0 nC? (1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
questions.why: E = Q/(4πε₀r²) = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁹/0.30² ≈ 200 N C⁻¹. Forgetting to square r gives 60.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V. How much kinetic energy does it gain? (e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.why: Work done by the field = QV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 500 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J (500 eV).

long.q: Two point charges of +3.0 nC and −5.0 nC are 4.0 cm apart in a vacuum. Calculate the magnitude of the electric force between them and state whether it is attractive or repulsive. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹)
scheme: C1: F = Qq ÷ (4πε₀r²)
B1: attractive (opposite charges)

long.q: Two parallel horizontal metal plates 15 mm apart have a potential difference of 600 V between them. Calculate the electric field strength between the plates, the force on an electron between them and its acceleration. Describe the path of an electron that enters the field midway between the plates moving parallel to them. (e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
scheme: A1: a = F ÷ m = 7.0 × 10¹⁵ m s⁻²
B1: path is a parabola curving towards the positive plate (constant force perpendicular to the initial velocity)

long.q: Define the electric potential at a point. Calculate the electric potential at a distance of 0.20 m from a point charge of +4.0 µC, and the work done in moving a charge of +2.0 nC from a point 0.40 m from the +4.0 µC charge to a point 0.20 m from it. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹)
scheme: B1: work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point
C1: V = Q ÷ (4πε₀r)
C1: potential at 0.40 m is 9.0 × 10⁴ V, so W = qΔV = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 9.0 × 10⁴

long.q: Compare the gravitational field of a point mass with the electric field of a point charge, giving two similarities and two differences.
scheme: B1: similarity: both field strengths follow an inverse-square law with distance (F ∝ 1/r²)
B1: similarity: both are radial fields, and potential is inversely proportional to r with zero potential at infinity
B1: difference: gravitational forces are always attractive; electric forces can be attractive or repulsive
B1: difference: gravitational force acts on mass, electric force acts on charge; or gravitational potential is always negative while electric potential can be positive or negative

long.q: A charged oil drop of mass 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary between two horizontal plates 8.0 mm apart with a potential difference of 500 V between them. Calculate the charge on the drop and the number of electron charges this represents. The drop carries a negative charge; state which plate is positive. (g = 9.81 m s⁻², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
scheme: M1: electric force balances weight: qV/d = mg
A1: 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, which is 3 electron charges
B1: the upper plate is positive, so the force on the negative drop is upwards

questions.q: A 100 µF capacitor is charged to 12 V. How much energy is stored?
What is the time constant of a 2.0 kΩ resistor and 50 µF capacitor?
Capacitors in parallel…
questions.why: In parallel, capacitances add.

questions.q: Two 4.0 µF capacitors are connected in series. What is their combined capacitance?
questions.why: In series 1/C = 1/4.0 + 1/4.0 = 1/2.0, so C = 2.0 µF; series capacitance is less than either one.

questions.q: What happens to the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor if a dielectric of relative permittivity ε_r = 3 is inserted between the plates?
o: The capacitance drops by a factor of 3
questions.why: C = ε_r ε₀ A / d; inserting a dielectric with ε_r = 3 increases the capacitance by a factor of 3.

long.q: A 470 µF capacitor is charged to 12 V and then discharged through a 2.0 kΩ resistor. Calculate the time constant and the potential difference after 1.0 s.
Define capacitance. A 220 µF capacitor is charged to a potential difference of 9.0 V. Calculate the charge stored and the energy stored, and explain why the energy stored is ½QV rather than QV.
scheme: B1: capacitance = charge stored per unit potential difference (C = Q/V)
B1: W = ½CV² = 8.9 × 10⁻³ J
B1: the energy is the area under the graph of potential difference against charge
B1: the potential difference rises from 0 to V as charge is added, so the average p.d. is V/2

long.q: A 2.0 µF capacitor and a 3.0 µF capacitor are connected in series, and this combination is connected in parallel with a 4.0 µF capacitor. A potential difference of 10 V is applied across the whole arrangement. Calculate the total capacitance, the charge on the 4.0 µF capacitor and the charge on the 2.0 µF capacitor.
scheme: C1: series pair: 1/C = 1/2.0 + 1/3.0, C = 1.2 µF
B1: charge on 4.0 µF = 4.0 × 10 = 40 µC
B1: charge on 2.0 µF = charge on series pair = 1.2 × 10 = 12 µC

long.q: An isolated metal sphere of radius 0.15 m is in air. Calculate its capacitance, and the charge on it when its potential is 50 kV. (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹)

A capacitor discharges through a resistor of resistance R = 4.7 kΩ ± 5%. It is suggested that the potential difference V across the capacitor varies with time t as V = V₀e^(−t/RC). State the graph that should be plotted to test this relationship and how RC and V₀ are found from it. The gradient of the student's line is found to be −0.42 ± 0.02 s⁻¹. Calculate C and its absolute uncertainty.
scheme: B1: plot ln V on the y-axis against t on the x-axis; a straight line supports the relationship
B1: gradient = −1/(RC)
B1: y-intercept = ln V₀, so V₀ = e^(intercept)
C1: percentage uncertainties add: 4.8% + 5% ≈ 10%

questions.q: What is the force on a 0.50 m wire carrying 3.0 A at right angles to a 0.20 T field?
A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field at right angles. Its path is…
questions.why: The force Bqv is always perpendicular to the velocity, giving circular motion.

questions.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of conservation of…
questions.why: The induced current opposes the change that caused it; otherwise energy would be created.

questions.q: According to Lenz's law, the direction of an induced e.m.f. is such that it:
o: Increases the rate of change of flux
Aligns with the external magnetic field
Opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it
questions.why: Lenz's law expresses conservation of energy: the induced current produces a field opposing the flux change.

questions.q: A coil of 200 turns and area 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is perpendicular to a 0.050 T magnetic field. The field falls uniformly to zero in 0.020 s. What is the average induced e.m.f.?
questions.why: Change in flux linkage = NBA = 200 × 0.050 × 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 4.0 × 10⁻³ Wb; e.m.f. = 4.0 × 10⁻³/0.020 = 0.20 V. Leaving out N gives 1.0 × 10⁻³ V.

long.q: An electron travels at 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 2.0 mT. Calculate the radius of its circular path. (e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
scheme: M1: Bqv = mv²/r so r = mv/(Bq)

long.q: Define the tesla. A straight wire of length 0.050 m carries a current of 4.0 A in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.15 T. Calculate the force on the wire when it is perpendicular to the field and when it is at 30° to the field, and state how the direction of the force is found.
scheme: B1: one tesla is the uniform flux density that produces a force of 1 N per metre on a wire carrying a current of 1 A at right angles to the field
C1: F = BIL sin θ
A1: perpendicular: F = 0.15 × 4.0 × 0.050 = 0.030 N
B1: Fleming's left-hand rule (force perpendicular to both the field and the current)

long.q: State Faraday's law and Lenz's law of electromagnetic induction. A coil of 200 turns and area 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ m² is perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.30 T. The field is reduced uniformly to zero in 0.050 s. Calculate the average e.m.f. induced, and explain how Lenz's law is a consequence of conservation of energy.
scheme: B1: Faraday: the induced e.m.f. is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage
B1: Lenz: the direction of the induced e.m.f. (current) is such as to oppose the change that produces it
B1: if the induced current aided the change, energy would be created without work being done; opposing it means work must be done, which becomes electrical energy

long.q: A slice of semiconductor 0.50 mm thick carries a current of 40 mA in a magnetic field of 0.25 T perpendicular to its faces. The number density of charge carriers is 1.2 × 10²⁴ m⁻³. Calculate the Hall voltage across the slice, and explain why the Hall voltage for a metal slice of the same size under the same conditions would be much smaller. (e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
scheme: C1: V_H = BI ÷ (ntq)
B1: a metal has a much larger number density of charge carriers, so for the same current the drift speed is much smaller and V_H ∝ 1/n is much smaller

long.q: A beam of positive ions enters a region where a uniform electric field of strength 3.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.060 T are perpendicular to each other and to the beam. Show that only ions of one particular speed pass through undeflected, calculate this speed, and state what happens to faster ions.
scheme: M1: undeflected when electric force = magnetic force: qE = Bqv
A1: v = E ÷ B, independent of the charge and mass of the ion
B1: faster ions have a magnetic force greater than the electric force, so they are deflected in the direction of the magnetic force

questions.q: A sinusoidal a.c. has a peak voltage of 325 V. What is its r.m.s. value?
What does a single diode do to a.c.?
questions.why: It lets current through in one direction only, removing half of each cycle.

questions.q: A sinusoidal alternating voltage has peak value 10 V. What is its r.m.s. value?
questions.why: V_rms = V₀ ÷ √2.

questions.q: A sinusoidal alternating current of peak value 2.0 A passes through a 100 Ω resistor. What is the mean power dissipated?
questions.why: Mean power = I_rms²R = (I₀²/2)R = (4.0/2) × 100 = 200 W. Using the peak current gives the peak power of 400 W.

questions.q: A capacitor smooths the output of a rectifier feeding a load resistor. What is the effect of using a larger capacitance?
o: The ripple decreases, because the time constant RC is larger
The ripple increases, because the capacitor stores more charge
questions.why: A larger C gives a larger time constant RC, so the capacitor discharges less between peaks and the ripple is smaller.

long.q: A sinusoidal alternating supply has a peak voltage of 325 V. Calculate its root-mean-square (r.m.s.) voltage. The supply is connected to a 50 Ω resistor; calculate the maximum power and the mean power dissipated in the resistor.
scheme: C1: V_rms = V₀ ÷ √2
A1: maximum power = V₀² ÷ R = 325² ÷ 50 = 2.1 × 10³ W
A1: mean power = V_rms² ÷ R = 1.06 × 10³ W (half the maximum)

long.q: Define the root-mean-square (r.m.s.) value of an alternating current, and explain why, for a sinusoidal current, the mean power in a resistor is half the maximum power.
scheme: B1: r.m.s. current is the value of the steady direct current that would dissipate energy at the same rate in a resistor
B1: power P = I²R and I² = I₀² sin² ωt varies between 0 and I₀²
B1: the mean value of sin² ωt over a cycle is ½, so the mean power is ½I₀²R, half the maximum, and I_rms = I₀/√2

long.q: Describe how a single diode produces half-wave rectification of an alternating voltage, and how four diodes in a bridge produce full-wave rectification. Describe the output voltage across the load in each case.
scheme: B1: a diode conducts in one direction only
B1: with a single diode in series with the load, current flows only during alternate half-cycles; the output is positive half-cycles with gaps of zero between them
B1: in a bridge, two diodes conduct during one half-cycle and the other two during the next
B1: current through the load is always in the same direction, so the output is a series of positive half-cycles with no gaps

long.q: A capacitor is connected in parallel with the load resistor at the output of a rectifier. Explain how the capacitor smooths the output voltage, and explain how the amount of ripple changes if a capacitor of larger capacitance is used.
scheme: B1: the capacitor charges up as the rectified voltage rises to its peak
B1: when the rectified voltage falls, the capacitor discharges through the load, maintaining the current and the voltage across it
B1: a larger capacitance gives a larger time constant RC
B1: so the capacitor discharges more slowly between peaks and the ripple is smaller

long.q: An alternating voltage V, in volts, is given by V = 17 sin(100πt), where t is in seconds. Determine the peak voltage, the frequency, the r.m.s. voltage, and the value of V when t = 2.5 ms.
scheme: B1: peak voltage = 17 V
B1: ω = 100π = 2πf, so f = 50 Hz

questions.q: The energy of a photon is E = hf. Doubling the frequency…
questions.why: E is proportional to f.

questions.q: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of light above the threshold frequency…
o: increases the maximum kinetic energy of electrons
increases the number of electrons emitted per second
questions.why: More photons per second release more electrons; each photon still has the same energy.

questions.q: Electron diffraction is evidence that electrons…
questions.why: Diffraction is a wave property; λ = h/p.

questions.q: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
questions.why: λ = h/(mv) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.0 × 10⁶) ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, comparable to atomic spacings.

questions.q: An electron in a hydrogen atom drops from the −3.4 eV level to the −13.6 eV level. What is the wavelength of the photon emitted? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.why: The photon energy is the difference, 10.2 eV = 1.63 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, so λ = hc/E ≈ 1.22 × 10⁻⁷ m = 122 nm.

long.q: Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.3 eV. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons in eV. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
scheme: C1: photon energy = hc/λ = 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

long.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 150 V. Calculate its de Broglie wavelength, and explain why a beam of such electrons is diffracted when it passes through a thin crystalline film. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
scheme: C1: kinetic energy = eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 150 = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁷ J
B1: moving electrons behave as waves
B1: their wavelength is similar to the spacing between atoms in the crystal, so significant diffraction occurs

long.q: Three energy levels of the hydrogen atom are −13.6 eV, −3.40 eV and −1.51 eV. Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted when an electron moves from the −3.40 eV level to the −13.6 eV level. Explain why the emission spectrum of hydrogen consists of discrete lines. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
scheme: C1: λ = hc ÷ ΔE
B1: electrons in atoms can only have discrete energy levels
B1: each photon is emitted when an electron falls between two levels, so it has a specific energy hf = E₁ − E₂ and hence a specific wavelength

long.q: Explain how the photoelectric effect provides evidence for the particulate nature of electromagnetic radiation. Refer to the threshold frequency and to the effect of intensity.
scheme: B1: emission occurs only above a threshold frequency, whatever the intensity; wave theory predicts any frequency would work given enough time
B1: one photon gives all its energy hf to one electron; below the threshold hf is less than the work function
B1: the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends on frequency, not intensity
B1: increasing intensity increases the number of photons per second and so the rate of emission (and emission is instantaneous)

long.q: A laser emits light of wavelength 633 nm with a power output of 5.0 mW. Calculate the energy of one photon and the number of photons emitted per second. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
scheme: A1: number per second = 5.0 × 10⁻³ ÷ 3.14 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.6 × 10¹⁶ s⁻¹

questions.q: Binding energy per nucleon is greatest for nuclei around…
questions.why: Iron-56 is near the peak; fusion of lighter and fission of heavier nuclei both release energy.

questions.q: A source has decay constant λ. Its half-life is…
What is the mass defect of a nucleus?
o: The mass lost in alpha decay
The difference between the mass of its separate nucleons and the mass of the nucleus
questions.why: It corresponds to the binding energy, E = Δm c².

questions.q: A source has an activity of 800 Bq and a half-life of 5.0 minutes. What is its activity 15 minutes later?
questions.why: 15 minutes is 3 half-lives, so the activity is 800 × (½)³ = 100 Bq. Dividing by 3 instead gives 267 Bq.

questions.q: A nucleus has a mass defect of 0.030 u. What is its binding energy? (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)

long.q: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 8.0 days. Calculate its decay constant and the fraction remaining after 20 days.

The mass of a helium-4 nucleus is 4.001506 u. The mass of a proton is 1.007276 u and the mass of a neutron is 1.008665 u. Calculate the mass defect of the helium-4 nucleus, its binding energy in joules and its binding energy per nucleon. (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
scheme: C1: mass of separate nucleons = 2 × 1.007276 + 2 × 1.008665 = 4.031882 u
A1: mass defect = 0.030376 u = 5.04 × 10⁻²⁹ kg
C1: E = Δmc²
A1: binding energy per nucleon = 1.1 × 10⁻¹² J

long.q: Use the variation of binding energy per nucleon with nucleon number to explain why energy is released both when a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 undergoes fission and when light nuclei such as hydrogen isotopes undergo fusion.
scheme: B1: binding energy per nucleon increases with nucleon number for light nuclei, reaches a maximum near iron (A ≈ 56), then decreases slowly for heavy nuclei
B1: in fission a heavy nucleus splits into two medium nuclei with greater binding energy per nucleon
B1: in fusion light nuclei combine into a nucleus with greater binding energy per nucleon
B1: in both cases the total binding energy increases (mass decreases) and the difference is released as energy

long.q: Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8.0 days and a molar mass of 0.131 kg mol⁻¹. Calculate the number of nuclei in a 1.0 µg sample and its activity. (Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
scheme: A1: A = λN = 4.6 × 10⁹ Bq

long.q: Radioactive decay is described as random and spontaneous. Explain what is meant by each of these terms, and describe what evidence for random decay is seen when the count rate from a source is measured with a Geiger–Müller tube.
scheme: B1: random: it is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or when a particular nucleus will decay (only a probability per unit time)
B1: spontaneous: decay is not affected by external factors such as temperature or pressure
B1: the count rate fluctuates about a mean value when repeated readings are taken

questions.q: In ultrasound imaging, a gel is used between the probe and skin to…
o: reduce reflection at the air boundary (match acoustic impedance)
questions.why: Air causes almost total reflection; gel matches impedances so ultrasound enters the body.

questions.q: PET scanning detects…
o: pairs of gamma photons from positron–electron annihilation
questions.why: A positron annihilates with an electron, emitting two gamma photons in opposite directions.

questions.q: Why is gel used between an ultrasound probe and the skin?
o: It matches acoustic impedance, so little ultrasound is reflected at the skin
questions.why: Air has a very different impedance from skin, so without gel most of the wave reflects.

questions.q: Ultrasound meets a boundary between soft tissue (Z = 1.6 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹) and bone (Z = 7.8 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹). What fraction of the incident intensity is reflected?
questions.why: I_R/I₀ = (Z₂ − Z₁)²/(Z₂ + Z₁)² = (6.2/9.4)² ≈ 0.44. Forgetting to square gives 0.66.

questions.q: X-rays are attenuated in a material with linear attenuation coefficient 0.50 cm⁻¹. What thickness halves the intensity?

long.q: A parallel beam of X-rays passes through 3.0 cm of bone or through 3.0 cm of soft tissue. The linear attenuation coefficient is 0.60 cm⁻¹ for bone and 0.18 cm⁻¹ for soft tissue. Calculate the fraction of the X-ray intensity transmitted in each case, and explain why bone shows up clearly against soft tissue on an X-ray image.
scheme: C1: I/I₀ = e^(−μx)
A1: soft tissue: e^(−0.54) = 0.58
B1: far more X-ray intensity reaches the detector through soft tissue than through bone
B1: the large difference in attenuation coefficients gives good contrast (a sharp difference in exposure between the regions)

long.q: The specific acoustic impedance of soft tissue is 1.63 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹ and that of bone is 7.80 × 10⁶ kg m⁻² s⁻¹. Calculate the intensity reflection coefficient for ultrasound at a soft tissue–bone boundary. Explain why a gel is applied between the ultrasound probe and the skin.
scheme: C1: α = (Z₂ − Z₁)² ÷ (Z₂ + Z₁)²
B1: without gel there is air between the probe and the skin; air has a very much smaller impedance, so almost all the ultrasound (about 99.9%) is reflected
B1: the gel has an impedance similar to skin, so very little is reflected and most is transmitted into the body

long.q: Describe how a piezo-electric transducer generates ultrasound and how the same transducer detects the reflected pulses in an ultrasound scan.
scheme: B1: an alternating potential difference is applied across a piezo-electric crystal
B1: the crystal changes shape (expands and contracts) at the frequency of the applied p.d.
B1: when this frequency is an ultrasonic frequency equal to the crystal's natural frequency it resonates, emitting ultrasound
B1: returning ultrasound makes the crystal vibrate, producing an alternating p.d. across it that is detected; the transducer emits short pulses and detects echoes between them

long.q: In PET scanning a tracer emits positrons. Explain how the gamma photons detected are produced, and why they travel in opposite directions. Calculate the energy of each gamma photon. (mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
scheme: B1: an emitted positron meets an electron in the body and they annihilate
B1: their combined mass is converted into the energy of two gamma photons
B1: the positron and electron have negligible momentum before, so to conserve momentum the photons move in opposite directions with equal energy
C1: energy of each photon = mₑc² = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)²

long.q: Describe how X-rays are produced in an X-ray tube. Calculate the minimum wavelength of X-rays produced by a tube operating at an accelerating potential difference of 80 kV, and explain why an aluminium filter is placed in the X-ray beam for medical imaging. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
scheme: B1: electrons accelerated through a high p.d. strike a metal target and decelerate rapidly, emitting X-ray photons (braking radiation)
C1: minimum wavelength when all the electron's energy forms one photon: eV = hc/λ_min
B1: the filter absorbs low-energy (long-wavelength) X-rays that would be absorbed by the body without reaching the detector, reducing the dose to the patient

questions.q: A standard candle is…
o: an object of known luminosity, used to find distances
questions.why: Knowing L and measuring the flux F gives the distance from F = L/4πd².

questions.q: Hubble's law states that the recession speed of a galaxy is proportional to…
questions.why: v = H₀d, evidence for an expanding Universe.

questions.q: Wien's displacement law: a hotter star's peak wavelength is…
questions.why: λmax ∝ 1/T, so hotter stars peak at shorter wavelengths (bluer).

questions.q: A spectral line emitted at 500.0 nm is observed in a galaxy's spectrum at 505.0 nm. What is the galaxy's recession speed? (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.why: Δλ/λ ≈ v/c, so v = (5.0/500.0) × 3.00 × 10⁸ = 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, moving away (redshift).

questions.q: Stars A and B have the same radius, but A's surface temperature is twice B's. What is the ratio of luminosities L_A/L_B?
questions.why: Stefan–Boltzmann: L = 4πr²σT⁴. With equal radii, doubling T multiplies L by 2⁴ = 16.

long.q: Explain what is meant by a standard candle. A standard candle has a luminosity of 4.0 × 10²⁸ W, and the radiant flux intensity received from it at the Earth is 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ W m⁻². Calculate its distance from the Earth.
scheme: B1: an astronomical object of known luminosity
M1: F = L ÷ (4πd²)

long.q: The spectrum of a star has its peak intensity at a wavelength of 500 nm, and the luminosity of the star is 3.8 × 10²⁶ W. Use Wien's displacement law to find the surface temperature of the star, then calculate its radius. (Wien constant = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K, σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴)
scheme: C1: λ_max T = 2.9 × 10⁻³ m K
C1: L = 4πσr²T⁴

long.q: A spectral line with a laboratory wavelength of 656.3 nm is observed at 669.4 nm in the light from a distant galaxy. Calculate the speed at which the galaxy is receding and use Hubble's law to estimate its distance. State what the redshift of distant galaxies suggests about the universe. (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, H₀ = 2.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ s⁻¹)
scheme: C1: Δλ ÷ λ = v ÷ c with Δλ = 13.1 nm
C1: d = v ÷ H₀
B1: distant galaxies are all moving away from us, so the universe is expanding

long.q: Explain how Hubble's law leads to the idea that the universe began with a Big Bang.
scheme: B1: Hubble's law states that the recession speed of a galaxy is proportional to its distance (v = H₀d)
B1: so, tracing their motion back in time, all galaxies were closer together in the past
B1: at some time in the past all matter was at a single point (very small, hot and dense), from which the universe expanded

long.q: Two stars A and B have the same surface temperature, but the luminosity of A is 16 times that of B. A third star C has the same radius as B but twice its surface temperature. Determine the ratio of the radius of A to the radius of B, and the ratio of the luminosity of C to the luminosity of B.
scheme: M1: L = 4πσr²T⁴, so at equal T, L ∝ r²
B1: at equal radius L ∝ T⁴, so L_C ÷ L_B = 2⁴ = 16
